transcript: The year is 1851 and in the city of London is taking place the first ever international chess tournament. The very best players of the time gather from all over Europe and amongst them there is a certain Adolf Anderssen from Germany. A player that is going to be remembered as the best player from the 1850s after winning that tournament. And the reason why I am telling you the outcome of that tournament is because the game that I'm going to show you today was not played as part of it. Instead, while all of these brilliant minds are battling it out in a small nearby cafe, Adolf Anderssen is just waiting for the next round to start while he gets to know another player. That player is called Lionel Kieseritzky, an incredibly strong chess player who has traveled from France. The two gentlemen decide to play a friendly game of chess with an old wooden set. But little do they know that game that they're about to play is going to be remembered centuries later as the Immortal Game. Adolf Anderssen opens with 1.e4 controlling the center.
